<explanation>
Below is a step‐by‐step explanation on how to create a compact yet thorough system design diagram for the MCP Unity Editor project. This project implements a bridge between Unity Editor (as a client/extension) and a Node.js backend server (implementing the Model Context Protocol), allowing AI assistants to interact with Unity. The diagram should clearly separate the main functional areas while keeping the composition tight and readable.

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Editor Component:
     - This folder (Editor/) contains all Unity Editor-specific code.
     - Subcomponents include:
       ▪ Resources (e.g., GetAssetsResource, GetConsoleLogsResource, GetGameObjectResource, etc.) that provide Unity’s data.
       ▪ Tools (e.g., AddAssetToSceneTool, AddPackageTool, RunTestsTool, etc.) that perform actions in the editor.
       ▪ UnityBridge that establishes communication channels between Unity and the server.
       ▪ Services (e.g., TestRunnerService) supporting backend interactions.
       ▪ Utility classes for configuration and workspace (McpConfigUtils, VsCodeWorkspaceUtils).
     
   • Server Component:
     - The Server/ directory houses the Node.js backend.
     - Contains:
       ▪ src folder with TypeScript sources for resources and tools mirroring the Editor functionality.
       ▪ Build folder with compiled JavaScript and type definitions.
       ▪ Package management artifacts (package.json) and Docker configuration for container deployment.
       ▪ Utility modules for error handling and logging.
   
   • External AI/LLM Clients:
     - Represented by connected AI coding assistants (Claude, Windsurf, Cursor) that interact via the WebSocket.
   
   • Communication Infrastructure:
     - WebSocket Server that facilitates real-time, bidirectional communications between the Editor and Node.js Server.
     - Environment configuration (e.g., UNITY_PORT) helps establish the proper ports and settings.

2. Define Relationships and Interactions:
   • The Unity Editor component (with its Tools, Resources, Services, and UnityBridge) communicates via a WebSocket to the Node.js server.
   • The Node.js Server acts as the central MCP server, handling incoming commands (e.g., execute_menu_item, select_gameobject):
     - It processes these requests (using resources and tools modules) and may perform operations back in the Unity Editor.
   • External AI clients connect to the Node.js server, sending instructions that are translated into actions within Unity.
   • Integration with IDEs (like VSCode) is enabled via configuration and package cache access.

3. Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
   • The separation of concerns is clear: Unity Editor (client-side functionality) and Node.js Server (backend communication layer) form a loosely coupled, distributed architecture.
   • The design employs a bridge pattern (visible in the UnityBridge module) to interact between Unity’s internal APIs and the external MCP protocol.
   • Technologies include Unity Editor’s C# environment and Node.js with TypeScript.
   • Communication patterns rely on real-time WebSocket data flows.

4. Guidelines for Drawing the Diagram (Keep the Composition Compact):
   • Use clearly labeled boxes to represent each component:
     - A box for the Unity Editor with labeled sub-boxes: Resources, Tools, Services, UnityBridge, and Utils.
     - A box for the Node.js Server with divisions for src (core logic), build (compiled output), configuration (package.json, Dockerfile), and utilities.
     - A box or cloud icon for the External AI Clients.
     - A distinct box or notation for the WebSocket communication channel.
   • Show directional arrows:
     - Arrows from External AI Clients to the Node.js Server.
     - Bi-directional arrows between the Unity Editor’s UnityBridge and the Node.js Server, indicating WebSocket connectivity.
     - Arrows from the Server to internal modules (resources, tools) depicting function calls.
   • Color-code or use different shapes:
     - Use one color/shape for Editor-side components and another for Server-side components.
     - Use dashed lines to illustrate configuration or optional deployment paths (like Docker).
   • Maintain compactness:
     - Rather than detailing every single submodule, group related items (for example, group all Tools together within both Editor and Server areas).
     - Focus on the core interactions and paths rather than an exhaustive breakdown.

5. Final Diagram Elements:
   • Components with clear labels:
     - “Unity Editor (Client)” with submodules: Resources, Tools, Services, UnityBridge, Utils.
     - “Node.js MCP Server” with submodules: Resources (mirrored), Tools (mirrored), Core, Utils, Build/Compilation Artifacts.
     - “External AI Clients” (Claude, Windsurf, Cursor) as interacting entities.
     - “WebSocket Channel” connecting Unity Editor and Node.js Server.
   • Directional flows:
     - Arrows indicating command flow from AI Clients → MCP Server.
     - Arrows showing bidirectional updates/notifications between Editor and Server.
   • Annotations:
     - Note the dependency on Node.js, Unity version, and the MCP protocol.
     - Briefly annotate the purpose (e.g., “Handles menu item execution”, “Manages asset and package operations”, etc.) alongside the depicted modules.

By following these guidelines, you will construct a compact and precise architectural diagram that effectively communicates the core components, interactions, and technologies of the MCP Unity project to fellow principal software engineers. This clear depiction will assist in understanding the integration between Unity Editor extensions and the Node.js backend, highlighting the essential architectural elements without over-complicating the visual. 
</explanation>
